analysis.one_liner: Rewrites California water rules to send more water to farms and cities during drought while loosening endangered-fish protections.
analysis.headline: The House passed it 245-176 on July 16, 2015, with 240 of 245 Republicans and 5 of 188 Democrats in favor, but the Senate never voted and the bill died when that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would rework how California's federal and state water projects run during drought: federal agencies would be required to deliver the maximum water supplies practicable to farm and city water contractors, and the Endangered Species Act protections for Delta smelt and salmon would be recalculated to allow more export pumping. It would also repeal a court-approved settlement to restore salmon on the San Joaquin River, speed up permitting for new dams, and add one disadvantaged community, Kettleman City, to the federal water service area. [S2, S3, S4]
analysis.who_benefits: The largest beneficiaries would be Central Valley agricultural water contractors and other State Water Project and Central Valley Project contractors, who would receive more exported water during drought years [S2, S4]. Municipal contractors and Kettleman City, which would get a contract for up to 900 acre-feet of drinking water, would also benefit [S4]. Water storage project developers would gain from streamlined federal permitting [S2].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Central Valley farm water districts and export contractors

how_it_helps.text: During drought years, the Agriculture, Commerce, and Interior departments would be required to approve projects and operations providing the maximum quantity of water supplies practicable to Central Valley Project and State Water Project contractors and other California water users [S2, S4].

The bill would rewrite how Delta smelt and salmon protections are calculated under the 2008 and 2009 biological opinions, directing agencies to manage export pumping to maximize water supplies and setting a default reverse-flow limit that allows more pumping than the agencies' current practice [S2, S3].

The bill repeals the San Joaquin River Restoration Settlement Act, ending the requirement to restore salmon on the San Joaquin River and deeming a warm-water fishery sufficient, which frees water for Friant Division farm contractors [S2, S4].

Kettleman City, a disadvantaged San Joaquin Valley community, would be added to the Central Valley Project service area with a contract for up to 900 acre-feet of municipal water when local supplies fall short [S4].

The bill speeds up water storage feasibility studies, makes the Bureau of Reclamation the lead agency coordinating permits for new storage projects, and sets deadlines for federal agencies to finish environmental reviews [S2].

analysis.who_pays: The costs would fall on endangered Delta smelt and salmon populations, whose protections would be loosened; on the commercial and recreational salmon fishing industry; on tribes and communities relying on the San Joaquin River restoration settlement and Trinity River flow commitments, which the bill caps [S2, S3, S4]. Water contractors themselves would cover the cost of the Stanislaus predator-removal program and climate study costs [S2].
analysis.who_pays_short: Endangered fish, salmon fisheries, and tribes

drawbacks.text: The bill would repeal the San Joaquin River Restoration Settlement Act and the court-approved settlement it implements, reneging on a decades-old legal agreement to restore salmon runs on the San Joaquin River [S2, S4].

It would prohibit federal agencies from distinguishing between naturally spawned and hatchery-spawned fish in Endangered Species Act determinations, a method that can inflate population counts of species listed as threatened or endangered [S2, S4].
It would allow agencies to deem projects in compliance with the National Environmental Policy Act during declared drought emergencies, waiving standard environmental review [S2, S4].

It would cap Trinity River restoration releases at 2000 record-of-decision volumes and could cut the annual quantity of Central Valley Project water dedicated to fish and wildlife purposes by 25% if project yield targets are not met [S4].

The bill's tightened standards, such as requiring written proof that a restriction is necessary before limiting pumping, could make it harder for fishery agencies to respond quickly as conditions change in the Delta [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill addresses real and documented drought hardship, including farm job losses and communities without reliable clean water [S2]. But its main mechanism is loosening Endangered Species Act protections and voiding a court settlement to move more water to large farm and city contractors, and the costs fall on fisheries, tribes, and the Delta ecosystem rather than on the water users who gain [S2, S3, S4]. The provisions aimed directly at ordinary people, chiefly the Kettleman City water contract, are narrow next to the agricultural water reallocation at the bill's core [S4].

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it on July 16, 2015, but the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee held one hearing and never brought it to a vote, and the bill died when the 114th Congress ended.

narrative.text: The House Natural Resources Committee reported the bill amended on a 23-12 vote on July 9, 2015 [S7].
The House passed the bill 245-176 on July 16, 2015, with 240 of 245 voting Republicans in favor and 5 of 188 voting Democrats in favor [S8].

Before passage, Democrats offered a motion to recommit instructing the committee to add guarantees of untainted residential drinking water, wildfire water supply, and protection of tribal water rights; it failed 183-239, with 183 Democrats in favor and 239 Republicans opposed [S7, S8].

The Senate received the bill on July 21, 2015 and referred it to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources, which held a hearing on October 8, 2015 but never reported the bill or voted on it [S7].
The 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017, without the Senate ever voting on the bill [S1, S7].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never became law, existing Endangered Species Act protections for Delta smelt and salmon, the San Joaquin River restoration settlement, and Trinity River flow requirements all remained in place. Large agricultural water contractors did not get the looser pumping rules the bill would have given them.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Delta fisheries and the settlement's beneficiaries

sides.party_line_note: House passage split sharply by party, 240 of 245 Republicans yes against 5 of 188 Democrats yes, and the motion to recommit was 183 Democrats yes to 239 Republicans no [S8].

industries.note: The bill's core purpose is to shift more of California's project water to large irrigation districts and export contractors during drought, easing the pumping restrictions now in place to protect Delta smelt and salmon [S2, S4]. Farm communities would gain crops and jobs, but the water comes from fishery protections and a restoration settlement that other communities and industries rely on [S3, S4].

Looser pumping rules, the repeal of the San Joaquin River restoration settlement, and caps on Trinity River releases would reduce the salmon populations the fishing industry depends on, a loss shared with consumers and river communities [S2, S4].

industries.industry: Municipal and industrial water users in California
industries.note: Urban water contractors and towns like Kettleman City would get more reliable municipal supplies and faster water transfers during drought [S4].

industries.industry: Water storage project developers and irrigation districts
industries.note: The bill speeds feasibility studies, makes Reclamation the lead permitting agency, allows nonfederal funding of permit reviews, and lets irrigation district joint powers authorities partner on new storage projects [S2].

industries.industry: Tribes with water and fisheries interests
industries.note: The bill bars federal agencies from conditioning permits on water rights in ways that affect tribes and caps Trinity restoration flows, while a floor amendment to guarantee tribal water rights failed [S2, S7].
